title: À mesa — at the restaurant
title_target: Queria a ementa, se faz favor
goal: Get through a whole dinner in Portuguese: arriving, ordering, asking what's in a dish, and paying — plus one Portuguese custom that surprises many tourists.
bekal: using *muito* and *pouco* correctly, both as adjectives and adverbs

dialogs.title: Diálogo — Numa tasca
dialogs.intro: Ana takes Budi to her family's favorite *tasca* — a small eatery with wooden tables and paper tablecloths.

notes: **A ementa, not o cardápio.** The menu in Portugal is *a ementa* or *a lista*; *cardápio* is the Brazilian word. A cheap fixed-price lunch is called *o prato do dia* or *a ementa turística*.

**Leva means "contains" when talking about food.** *Leva carne?* = "does it have meat in it?", *não leva açúcar* = "there's no sugar in it". It's a must-know question if you have dietary restrictions. To make it clear: *Sou vegetariano* or *Não como carne de porco*.

**Vinho tinto, not vinho vermelho.** Red wine is always *tinto*; *vermelho* is never used for wine. Its partners: *vinho branco* (white) and *vinho verde* — which isn't green at all, but a young, slightly sparkling wine from northern Portugal.
**Depois vemos** = "we'll see later". A short, very useful phrase for putting off a decision without saying no.
**Junto a** means "next to" or "by", and it contracts like other prepositions: *junto à janela*, *junto ao rio*.
**A tasca** is a small, cheap, honest family eatery — Portugal's best-loved culinary institution. If you want to eat like a local, look for a tasca full of Portuguese people at one in the afternoon.

grammars.title: How to order
body: There are four structures, all polite and all used. Only one to avoid: *quero*, which sounds too blunt in Portugal.
after: *Queria* and *gostaria* are both past or conditional forms used for the present — Portuguese's way of softening a request, just as English turns "I want" into "I'd like".
To call a passing waiter, just say *Se faz favor!* or *Desculpe!* — don't call out *garçon* (that's French) or snap your fingers.

grammars.title: Muito and pouco — sometimes they change, sometimes not
body: These two words work both as adjectives and as adverbs, and only one of those roles changes form.
after: Look at the second row: *a comida é muito boa* — *muito* stays the same, while *boa* changes. Beginners get this wrong very often, because two words side by side behave differently. It's the difference between English "much/many" and "very".
Similar words: *algum / alguma* (some), *nenhum / nenhuma* (none, no), *todo / toda* (whole, all), *outro / outra* (other). All of them agree with the noun in gender and number.

grammars.title: One dinner, from arrival to departure
body: The sequence of phrases is almost always the same, so learn it as one routine.

head: Stage
Português
rows: *Boa noite, mesa para dois, se faz favor.*
*Qual é o prato do dia?* / *O que me recomenda?*
*Para mim, o bacalhau. E para beber, uma água.*

after: *O que me recomenda?* ("what do you recommend?") is one sentence that will transform your meals in Portugal. Tasca waiters almost always answer honestly, and often suggest something that isn't on the menu.

blocks.text: Several words in this table traveled to Asia with Portuguese sailors and live on in Indonesian almost unchanged: *a manteiga* → **mentega**, *o queijo* → **keju**, and *o bacalhau* → **bakalau**, still sold in Indonesian markets. Add *o garfo* → **garpu** (fork), and Budi's dinner table back home is practically Portuguese.

blocks.title: Three Portuguese table customs
items: **O couvert.** As soon as you sit down, the waiter puts bread, butter, olives, sometimes cheese on the table without your ordering it. It's **not free** — if you eat it, it goes on the bill. If you don't want it, just say *Não, obrigado* and they'll take it away. It's not a scam; it's a legitimate local custom.

**Mealtimes.** Lunch in Portugal is between 12:30 and 2:30 pm, dinner between 7:30 and 10:00 pm. Outside those hours, many kitchens are closed. Turning up for dinner at six means eating alone — or not eating at all.
**Tipping.** It's not compulsory and not expected on the American scale. Rounding up the bill or leaving five to ten percent in a good restaurant is more than enough.
